questions.prompt: The agent finished and reports a 2,000-line change across 40 files. What is your first move?
questions.explain: A change you cannot review is a change you cannot trust. Reduce it to pieces you can.

options.text: Do not accept one big change. Ask for a plan and small pieces, each with a check
Read the agent's summary and merge it if every claim in it sounds right
options.misconception: The summary is the agent's description of its own work. It is a claim, not evidence.

options.text: Read all 2,000 lines carefully tonight and merge once you reach the end
options.misconception: Review quality drops as volume grows, so you will approve things you did not really read.

options.text: Run the whole test suite and merge the change if everything passes
options.misconception: Passing tests on a 40-file change prove little, and the agent may have weakened the tests. You still cannot review the change.

questions.prompt: Put a review-budget routine in order.
questions.explain: Plan small, define success first, run it yourself, then review and keep each piece.
items: Ask for a plan before any code
Split the work into small reviewable pieces
Decide how you will check each piece
Review the piece, then commit it

why.Split the work into small reviewable pie: You need the plan before you can split it into pieces.
why.Decide how you will check each piece: Decide the check before you see the result, so you cannot rationalise afterwards.
why.Run the checks yourself: Run the checks after the piece exists.
why.Review the piece, then commit it: Commit after review, so each commit is something you vouch for.
why.Ask for a plan before any code: A plan first lets you redirect cheaply, before a wall of code exists.

questions.prompt: This is the agent's summary of its change. Which line should make you stop?
questions.explain: Deleting failing tests makes 'all tests pass' true and meaningless. Always check what happened to the tests.

lines.why: A plausible, checkable claim about scope.
A normal change that you can inspect in its own small diff.
This is only meaningful if the tests were not weakened. See the line above.

questions.prompt: Before you ask a collaborator to review AI-assisted work, who does each job?
questions.explain: Review is a shared check. The author owns the first pass.

items.text: Read your own diff and delete what you do not understand
items.misconception: If you have not read it, you are asking someone else to be the first reader.

items.text: Run the tests and the pipeline on the mock data
items.misconception: Running the checks is cheap for you and costs a collaborator an afternoon.

items.text: Tell them which parts the agent wrote
items.misconception: Disclosure lets the reviewer aim their attention. Hiding it makes their job harder.

items.text: Independently judge whether the approach is sound for the project
items.misconception: A second opinion on design is what review is for. It is not for catching typos you could have caught.

questions.prompt: A chunk of the agent's code works, but you cannot explain what it does. What now?
questions.explain: Code you cannot explain is a Black-box husk. If you cannot explain it back, simplify or drop it.

options.text: Get an explanation, then say it back yourself. If you cannot, simplify or drop it
Keep it for now: it works on the test input, so you can understand it later
options.misconception: 'It works' on one input does not mean you can maintain, debug or defend it.

options.text: Ask the agent to add comments to it and merge it once they read well
options.misconception: Comments are the agent's own account of the code and can be wrong. You still cannot explain it yourself.

options.text: Ask a second AI model to check it, and keep it if the second model agrees
options.misconception: A second model can share the same blind spots. The test is whether you can explain it, not whether another model nods.

questions.prompt: Match each enemy to the habit that defeats it.
questions.explain: Each enemy is a failure of checking or ownership, and each habit gives the check or ownership back.

pairs.right: Small pieces and a review budget
pairs.misconception: Volume is beaten by refusing to take it in one go.
A false claim is beaten by checking it against something the agent did not write.
Pushing work onto others is beaten by owning the first pass.

pairs.right: Explain it back, or drop it
pairs.misconception: Code nobody understands is beaten by understanding it, or removing it.

questions.prompt: A workflow asks a person to approve each of several hundred agent edits an hour. What is the problem, in the AI for Science draft's terms?
questions.explain: At that volume approval turns into click-through. A stated human check only counts as oversight when it shows what changed at a readable volume and allows edit, veto and stop.

options.text: Approval at that rate becomes rubber-stamping
None, since a person approved every item
options.misconception: Approval without scrutiny is not oversight; the draft says not to automate approval.

options.text: People are too slow, so the step should be removed
options.misconception: The draft keeps a real decision point where results or others are affected, and asks you to design it to fit the volume.

options.text: It matters only if some of the edits turn out to be wrong
options.misconception: The check has to work before you know which edits are wrong.
